A.explanation: Subtracts about $2 \text{kPa}$ from $101 \text{kPa}$. The gas side level is lower, so gas pressure must be greater than atmospheric pressure.

B.explanation: Uses only the $10.2 \text{ cm}$ height to get about $1 \text{kPa}$ and subtracts it. The pressure difference depends on the difference in levels, not one height alone.

C.explanation: Adds only the $10.2 \text{ cm}$ water column, about $1 \text{kPa}$, to $101 \text{kPa}$. The effective height is $31.4 \text{ cm} - 10.2 \text{ cm}$.

D.explanation: Adds $\rho g h$ for a $21.2 \text{ cm}$ water column, about $2.1 \text{kPa}$, to $101 \text{kPa}$ to give about $103 \text{kPa}$.

hints: Notice which water surface is higher: the open-to-atmosphere side is higher than the gas-tap side, so the gas pressure pushes harder than the atmosphere.
Find the vertical difference between the two water surfaces using $31.4 \text{ cm}$ and $10.2 \text{ cm}$ measured from the same bottom level, then convert it to metres.
Connect that height difference $h$ to pressure difference with $\Delta p = \rho g h$ using $\rho = 1000 \text{ kg m}^{-3}$ and add it to $101 \text{ kPa}$.
walkthrough: Identify the manometer levels from the diagram: open side is $31.4 \text{ cm}$ above the bottom datum and gas side is $10.2 \text{ cm}$ above the same datum.
Calculate the difference in height: $h = 31.4 \text{ cm} - 10.2 \text{ cm} = 21.2 \text{ cm} = 0.212 \text{ m}$. This water column balances the excess of gas pressure over atmospheric pressure.
State the hydrostatic pressure rule: $\Delta p = \rho g h$, where $\rho = 1000 \text{ kg m}^{-3}$ and $g = 9.81 \text{ m s}^{-2}$.

Substitute values with units: $\Delta p = 1000 \times 9.81 \times 0.212 \approx 2080 \text{ Pa} \approx 2.1 \text{ kPa}$. Unit check gives $\text{kg m}^{-3} \times \text{m s}^{-2} \times \text{m} = \text{Pa}$.
Add to atmospheric pressure because the gas pushes the open side up: $p_{gas} = 101 \text{ kPa} + 2.1 \text{ kPa} \approx 103 \text{ kPa}$. This is option D.
